Chapter 2: Laying the Groundwork—Preparation Before Approaching Investors
Before you reach out to potential investors, there’s some groundwork that really can’t be skipped. It’s not just about getting your paperwork in order—it’s about understanding the heart of your business, what you truly need, and making sure you’ve got the right team and story to back it all up.
Let’s start with defining your funding need. Think of it like planning a big road trip. You wouldn’t just guess how much gas you’ll need or where you’re going, right? So, look ahead over the next twelve to eighteen months. What are the big milestones you want to hit—maybe it’s a product launch, hitting a certain number of users, or hitting a revenue goal? Figure out what resources you’ll need to get there.
If you ask for too much—investors might wonder if you’re overestimating. Too little, and you could seem unprepared. Getting this number right shows you’ve put real thought into your plan.
Now, let’s talk about building a strong team. Investors often say they invest in people more than just ideas. So, you want a team that brings together different skills—maybe some folks are strong on the technical side, others are business-minded, and someone else is great at marketing.
It also helps to have a track record of actually getting things done. And everyone should know their roles. If you spot gaps, don’t wait—think about bringing in an advisor or even a new co-founder to fill those spaces and boost your team’s credibility.
Next up, crafting a compelling story. This is your chance to connect with investors on an emotional level. What problem are you solving? Why does it matter? How is your team the one to fix it? Your story should be simple, real, and easy to remember.
Root it in real-world problems—maybe you’ve got some customer feedback or early traction to back it up. If your story is strong, it’s so much easier for investors to see your potential and catch your passion.
Of course, you’ll also need to prepare key materials. Think of your pitch deck as your business’s highlight reel—ten to fifteen slides that cover the problem, your solution, the market, your business model, your team, and your numbers.
You’ll also want an executive summary—a quick, one- or two-page overview—and some solid financial projections that show you’ve done your homework. And if you can, a demo or prototype can really bring your idea to life.
Just remember, keep these materials clear, easy to follow, and designed for your audience. Don’t drown them in jargon or details—they want to see the big picture.
Now, here’s something a lot of founders overlook: do your own due diligence on investors. It’s not just about who has money. You want investors who really get your space—folks who’ve invested in your stage, sector, or region. Check out their reputation. Talk to other founders who’ve worked with them.
The right investors are partners who share your vision, not just check-writers.
There’s also the legal and structural side to think about. Before you start fundraising, make sure your business is set up properly—usually that means incorporating as a Delaware C-corp if you’re in the US. Get your founder shares and cap table in order, and protect your intellectual property with trademarks or patents if you have them.
Doing this early helps avoid headaches down the road and shows investors you’re serious.
And finally—set realistic expectations. Fundraising almost never happens overnight. It takes time, persistence, and a thick skin for rejection. Every meeting, every bit of feedback—it’s all a chance to learn and refine your pitch.
Stick with it, stay adaptable, and keep your eyes on the goal.
